final_answer:
Short answer: No on both points, assuming the Lease is a 'finance lease' under Virginia's UCC Article 2A (Va. Code Title 8.2A). Client cannot stop paying Lessor, and Lessor is not responsible for the defective Trailers. Client's remedy lies against Manufacturer, which as a practical matter means a claim in the Chapter 7 case.

1. Finance-lease status. Under Va. Code 8.2A-103 a finance lease is one where (i) the lessor does not select, manufacture or supply the goods; (ii) the lessor acquires the goods in connection with the lease; and (iii) one of several conditions is met, including that the lessee received a copy of the supply contract before signing the lease. Each element is met here. Client picked the model and negotiated the refrigeration specs with Manufacturer, so Lessor did not 'select' the goods. Lessor is a financier that bought the Trailers only to lease them to Client. Client got a complete copy of the purchase agreement, including the warranty, before signing. Client is a business and not a consumer, so the consumer-lease carve-outs do not apply. (Caveat: I could only confirm the 8.2A-103 text through a search-engine summary of the official Virginia page, and I could not read the full text of the subsection. I rely on the standard UCC 2A-103(1)(g)(iii)(A) formulation.)

2. Payments are irrevocable and independent. Va. Code 8.2A-407 provides that, for a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee's promises under the lease become irrevocable and independent upon acceptance of the goods. The Lease's 'absolute and unconditional' clause, which waives defenses, setoff, counterclaim and recoupment, is the usual hell-or-high-water clause and is consistent with the statute. Client accepted and used the Trailers for four months, and so it must keep paying even though the goods are defective and Manufacturer has failed. Withholding payment is a lease default, exposing Client to Lessor's default remedies under Part 5 (acceleration if the Lease provides it, repossession, damages, and attorney fees if the Lease provides them).

3. No revocation of acceptance against Lessor. Under UCC 2A-516 and 2A-517 as enacted generally, a finance lessee that is not a consumer cannot revoke acceptance because of a defect in the goods. The only revocation right is where the lessor itself defaults. Here the lessor has not defaulted, because it delivered the goods the supplier supplied. I confirmed this from the uniform text and from the D.C., Nebraska and other enactments surfaced in search. I did not read Virginia's own 8.2A-516 and 8.2A-517 text, because the official site was blocked. I assume Virginia follows the uniform text, which is typical, but that is not verified.

4. Lessor is not liable for the defects. Va. Code 8.2A-212 states the implied warranty of merchantability applies 'except in a finance lease', and the UCC 2A-213 fitness warranty is likewise excluded for finance leases. The Lease contains no express Lessor warranty, and Client received a copy of the supply contract and was told to look to Manufacturer. Under the 2A-209 and 2A-407 scheme, a finance lessee's remedies for defects lie against the supplier. The lessor owes only limited warranties, such as against interference and infringement, none of which is implicated here.

5. Client's rights run against Manufacturer. Va. Code 8.2A-209 extends to the finance lessee the benefit of the supplier's promises and warranties under the supply contract, 'subject to the terms of the warranty and of the supply contract and all defenses or claims arising therefrom.' Client may therefore enforce the two-year warranty (the failures occurred at four months) directly against Manufacturer. But Manufacturer is in Chapter 7. Client should file a proof of claim for breach of warranty and repair damages, and should check for insurance or product-liability coverage, any extended or component-manufacturer warranties on the compressors (for example from the compressor or refrigeration-unit maker), and any third-party guarantee. These claims will probably recover cents on the dollar. Client should also give timely notice of the breach under 8.2A-516 and keep records. Any repair costs and downtime damages are Client's loss against Manufacturer, not Lessor.

6. Possible exceptions. (a) Lessor's separate misconduct, such as misrepresentation, fraud, or an agreement or course of dealing under which Lessor undertook responsibility for the goods, is not covered by the hell-or-high-water rule. Nothing in the facts suggests any such conduct. (b) If any element of the finance-lease definition fails (for example, if Lessor in fact selected or supplied the Trailers, or Client did not receive the supply contract before signing), the Lease would be an ordinary lease. Then the implied warranties and the revocation rights against Lessor could be available, subject to any valid disclaimer. The facts as given foreclose this. (c) The Lease itself may contain a provision on acceleration, remedies, or a 'true lease' versus security-interest characterization (Va. Code 8.1A-203), and this analysis did not review those terms. With 60 months at $2,200 per trailer ($132,000 per trailer), against a purchase price of $85,000, the structure is most likely a lease intended as security if the term equals the economic life or there is a nominal purchase option. That would not change the hell-or-high-water analysis, but it would change Lessor's remedies under UCC Article 9. (d) The Lessor's default remedies were not researched in detail. (e) Bankruptcy: Manufacturer's Chapter 7 does not affect Client's duty to Lessor.

Bottom line: Client should resume payment, cure arrears and fully reserve its rights, then pursue Manufacturer's estate and other sources. A negotiated forbearance or a settlement with Lessor, or an arrangement for replacement trailers, is the only practical way to reduce payments. Lessor has no legal obligation to give one. Verification limits: Virginia's official code site and most statute sites were blocked by the research proxy, so statutory text was confirmed through search summaries, not from full-text reads, and I did not locate Virginia case law applying these sections.

claims.text: The Lease qualifies as a non-consumer finance lease because Client selected the Trailers and negotiated specs, Lessor only financed them, and Client received the supply contract before signing.

Upon acceptance, Client's payment obligations became irrevocable and independent, so Client cannot withhold payments because of the defects or Manufacturer's bankruptcy; the Lease clause is consistent with the statute.
Lessor is not liable for defects: the implied warranty of merchantability does not apply in a finance lease, and the Lease has no Lessor warranty.
Client's remedies run against Manufacturer as beneficiary of the supply-contract warranty, which is now collectible only as a claim in the Chapter 7 case.
Client cannot revoke acceptance against a non-defaulting Lessor in a non-consumer finance lease.
